sources.citation: Schokkin, Dineke. 2014. A grammar of Paluai, the language of Baluan Island, Papua New Guinea. PhD thesis, James Cook University, Cairns. xxvi+548 pp. DOI 10.25903/tpm1-j309. (Open thesis version of Schokkin 2020, A Grammar of Paluai, Pacific Linguistics 663, De Gruyter Mouton.)
sources.note: Nothing about Penchal. The only Penchal mention is Ross 1988's subgroup membership. The stress chapter (2.3.1, with subsections on di-, tri- and quadrisyllabic forms and 'Interaction of morphology and stress assignment') describes Paluai only and draws no comparison with Penchal or other Rambutyo languages.

sources.citation: Smythe, W.E. (ed. A. Healey). 1970. Melanesian, Micronesian, and Indonesian features in languages of the Admiralty Islands. Pacific Linguistics C-13:1209-1234.
sources.note: Rambutyo only on the map; the stress note (n.13) is about Gele' (Kele), not Penchal.

sources.citation: Wikipedia (en): Penchal language.
sources.note: Stub citing Ethnologue only; no bibliography leads.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 2021. Counting in the Admiralty Islands. Language & Linguistics in Melanesia 39: 19-55. (Glottolog ref 586201.)
sources.note: Penchal numerals (sǝw, lup, tulup, karu-tulup.., tiŋi-hul '20', liŋihul '30', topol '50') in plain transcription; discussion is morphological (quinary tens, borrowing); no stress marks and no prosodic remark for Penchal (a full-text search for stress/accent: no line with both 'Penchal' and 'stress').

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 2021. Eight Languages of the Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea. LLM Special Issue 2021: front matter and Introduction pp. 1-17; Sketch 8 Nauna pp. 547-622; Sketch 6 Loniu.
sources.note: Penchal is not one of the eight sketched languages (Table 0.1: 7.5 contact hours, 3 days); intro p.11 names no publication on Penchal; Nauna phonology section does not mention Penchal. No Penchal stress statement.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 2021. Sketch 7: Pak. In Eight Languages of the Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea, 481-546. Language & Linguistics in Melanesia Special Issue 2021.
sources.note: Stress remarks concern Pak only; Penchal appears solely as comparanda in 7.7 'The linguistic position of Pak' (numerals, PSEA lexical innovations). Nothing on Penchal stress.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 2013. The Austronesian languages. Revised edition. Asia-Pacific Linguistics Open Access Monographs A-PL 008. Canberra: Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, ANU. hdl:1885/10191.
sources.note: Segmental only for Penchal: 'several of the languages of Manus in the Admiralty Islands have contrastive medial geminates. These include at least Nali, Pelipowai, Mondropolon, Kele, Drehet, Levei, Likum, Lindrou, and Penchal' (p.231); Penchal subtractive numerals 7-9 (Table 5.11); *t > r flapping in eastern Admiralties incl. Penchal. The only Admiralties stress remarks concern Wuvulu (penultimate with rightward shift under suffixation) and Lindrou (apparent secondary phonemic stress); nothing on Penchal stress or tone.

sources.citation: Chan, Eugene S.L. (comp.). 2006 [data 1998]. Penchal, Manus, Papua New Guinea. In: Numeral Systems of the World's Languages (web database hosted by MPI-EVA Leipzig). Data supplied by Robert Blust (2 April 1998) and, for 11-2000, John Palek (Lenkau speaker, University of Papua New Guinea, 25 June 1998). Page dated 2006-10-23.
sources.note: Nothing. Numeral forms 1-2000 in IPA-like transcription without any stress or tone marking; the 'Other comments' paragraph describes only the decimal 'Manus type' system with subtractive 7-9 and Nauna-like tens, and gives c.1,000 speakers on Rambutyo. Temporary copy parsed at work_2026-09-20/disc3/penc1239/chan_Penchal.htm (not kept as a source).

sources.citation: Lynch, John, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley (eds.). 2002. The Oceanic Languages. Richmond: Curzon.
sources.note: Penchal mentioned only in a preverbal-particle example and the language listing; no sketch, nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 1998. A Lou vocabulary, with phonological notes. In D. Tryon (ed.), Papers in Austronesian Linguistics No. 5, 35-99. Pacific Linguistics A-92.
sources.note: Sec. 2.4.3 STRESS (p.57) describes Lou (final ~ penultimate in citation forms). Penchal cited only as Southeast Admiralty comparanda in the diachronic sections (e.g. p.69 flapping of *t absent in Penchal). Nothing on Penchal stress.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 1996. The linguistic position of the Western Islands, Papua New Guinea. In John Lynch & Fa'afo Pat (eds.), Oceanic Studies: Proceedings of the First International Conference on Oceanic Linguistics, 1-46. Pacific Linguistics C-133. Canberra: Australian National University. hdl:1885/253852.
sources.note: Stress is described for Wuvulu and Aua (penultimate, optional initial in trisyllabic bases, stress shift under suffixation) and for Seimat ('generally falls on the penultimate syllable'), i.e. other languages (wuvu1239, seim1238). Penchal: speaker count, the remark that POc *-p- has not lenited in 'Baluan, Lou, Penchal, and perhaps some other languages of the south-eastern Admiralties', and c.20 cognate-set reflexes (mina- 'hand', mosim, ciw 'needle', cay, pWicik, kal, kulul 'thunder', wati, cinal, mWamwan, alil, pehin, kew, kotay 'cuscus') in plain transcription without stress marks. Nothing…

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 1991. Sound change and migration distance. In Robert Blust (ed.), Currents in Pacific Linguistics: Papers on Austronesian languages and ethnolinguistics in honour of George W. Grace, 27-42. Pacific Linguistics C-117. Canberra: Australian National University. hdl:1885/253742.
sources.note: No prosody anywhere in the paper. Penchal occurs once, in the list of Admiralty languages whose reflex of POc *p is [p]/[h] (erosion value 1.0: '.. Pak-Tong, Lenkau, Penchal, Nauna, Patpatar'); the text searched for stress/accent/tone/syllable/prosod- has no hits at all.

sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL6201 .R67 1988
sources.note: Penchal appears only in sound-correspondence tables and cognate sets; no statement about Penchal stress (the only Glottolog reference for penc1239).

sources.citation: Schooling, Stephen & Janice Schooling. 1988. A preliminary sociolinguistic and linguistic survey of Manus Province. Pacific Linguistics A-76:211-241.
sources.note: Penchal: cognate percentages, village list, and one vowel remark (Penchal has a close central spread vowel and a front half-close rounded vowel). No stress statement for any language beyond generalities; nothing on Penchal stress.

sources.citation: Healey, Alan. 1976. Austronesian languages: Admiralty Islands area. In S.A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 2: Austronesian languages, 349-364. Pacific Linguistics C-39. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-C39.349.
sources.note: No phonology content: history of classification (Moseley, Meyer, Smythe, Schwartz, Blust), a compromise classified list of languages with villages and populations (Penchal, Rambutyo I., 400?), map and bibliography. No remarks on sounds or prosody of any language.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 1975 [deposited 2014]. Field packets RB2-011, Admiralty Islands survey: Penchal packet pp. 247-259 (lang. no. 16; speakers Ananche Kepui 15 and Moal Lapeap 14, Penchal village; 28-29 Mar and 1 Apr 1975, 7.5 contact hours). Kaipuleohone, University of Hawai'i, hdl:10125/33171.
sources.note: PRIMARY DATA ONLY, no prose statement. Handwritten phonetic transcriptions with sporadic acute accents, mixed placement: final (sangahul 'ten', tingihul '20', kalesul, motanput, polam, rahuy, pahew, ahay), penultimate (kamatu?, ratu?, rahot, wame, koko?, panu?, mosal, kesut, alang, macaw, puli?, uli?, kalap), initial in some trisyllables (kurupis, awaras, kunahal, moluan, pakeaw). Pages 247, 248, 252 viewed.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 1975. Penchal field packet, Kaipuleohone RB2-011 pp. 247-259 (high-resolution JPGs) plus cassette RB1-005 side 2 counter 192 'Penchal' (audio of the elicitation).
sources.note: The entire first-hand Penchal corpus (7.5 h); a systematic tally of Blust's stress diacritics on the hi-res scans, checked against the audio, is the only route to a stress statement short of new fieldwork. Low-res scans already held by the project.
